 FAFSA season
 Sara Maley , Staff Writer 
 • 
 November 16, 2026 
 Wikimedia Commons 
 The FAFSA season began earlier this fall as the 2027-28 school year applications have opened for rising and current college students. 
 The FAFSA, short for Federal Student Aid, is the main application used by the federal government to find out how much money — in the form of loans, grants, and work-studies — should be offered to each individual student. Factors such as family income, age, race and gender are used to determine the amount of financial aid awarded.  
 To complete the application, the student must create their Federal Student Aid (FSA) ID, gather required information and then fill out the form as accurately as possible in order to qualify for as much aid as possible. The online application is available on the official US Department of Education website, or at fafsa.gov . 
 Ella Williams, a junior at Guilford College, feels as though the application is difficult. “I don’t feel knowledgeable enough to really help someone else do it,” she said.  
 While Williams is able to do her own application, it isn’t without help. Her mother plays a part in the process as extra support, something she would advise other students to seek. “I would probably refer them [to the financial aid office].” 
 The Financial Aid Office, located in Hege Library, is used to extend affordability towards Guilford students and work with them  to create aid packages that allow students to go to college. 
 “We’re trying to put as much communication out there for students,” Tiana Chamberlain-Archie, a staff member at the financial aid office, said. 
 Financial aid and FAFSA propel students towards college by making it potentially more affordable to them. Furthermore, FAFSA can provide students with a credit score. By taking out loans from the federal government through the FAFSA and paying them back, college students create credit scores, allowing them to get credit cards and take out loans for businesses later on in life. 
 “[W]e’re trying to get the students to come [to the FAFSA information events] by any means possible,” Chamberlain-Archie said, “we need the students to do their FAFSA.” 
 To do so, the financial aid office is hosting FAFSA sessions to provide information, QR code hand-outs, financial aid virtual events and FAFSA drop-ins where students can stop by the financial aid office for help completing their application.  
 The financial aid office has started events early this year because “a lot of students wait till the last moment,” Chamberlain-Archie said. 
 The aid amount a student gets each year changes as well which is why the Federal Student Aid and the financial aid office recommends college students to get their FAFSA applications in as early as possible. 
  “When it gets to next year around May/June… ‘they’re like, where’s my aid?” Chamberlain-Archie said. 
 Ultimately, as the FAFSA application period begins, the financial aid office is encouraging students to complete the process early and seek assistance if needed. By getting a head start on the next academic year, students can receive help in navigating the year ahead.
